\chapter{Asking, and Asking Why}
\label{ch:ka-asking-why}
\hlchaptermodality{69}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can turn any Kannada statement into a question, ask for agreement, and ask why.}

Complete KA-C69-why and ask a yes-or-no question, a tag question and a why question in a row.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ū]{\kn{ೂ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S136-vowel-sign-uu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಅ} — which way did the pen travel first?

One character this time — a mark rather than a letter, and one that has quietly been changing the meaning of whole sentences.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ೂ}}
\textbf{\kn{ೂ}} — \emph{ū}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}, not a letter: it never stands alone. Hang it on a consonant and the built-in \emph{a} becomes a long \textbf{ū}. You have had the full letter \kn{ಊ} for the start of a word; this is the same sound, worn inside one.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ೂ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನಾನೂ}} \emph{nānū} — I too, from the joining lesson
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹೂವು}} \emph{hūvu} — a flower
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಮೂಗು}} \emph{mūgu} — the nose
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಕೂದಲು}} \emph{kūdalu} — hair
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ೂ}}
Put your pen on \kn{ೂ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{ೂ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ನಾನೂ}  ·  \kn{ಹೂವು}  ·  \kn{ಮೂಗು}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ೂ} three times, saying \emph{ū} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{ೂ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ೂ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ū}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gottā]{\kn{ಗೊತ್ತಾ} (gottā) — do you know?}

\label{lesson:KA-C69-is-it}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: which sign did you trace last, and what does \emph{gottilla} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಗೊತ್ತಾ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಗೊತ್ತಾ}} (\emph{gottā}) — \textquotedblleft{}do you know?\textquotedblright{}

It is \kn{ಗೊತ್ತು} with its ending swapped for a long \textbf{-\kn{ಆ}} (\emph{-ā}), and that ending is the whole question. Nothing else moved: no word order changed, nothing was added in front.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one ending turns any statement into a question}]
Put \textbf{-\kn{ಆ}} on the end of a statement and the statement becomes a yes-or-no question. That is the entire machinery.

You have been saying it since the third chapter without being told, inside \textbf{\kn{ನೀವು} \kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ}} (\emph{nīvu hēgiddīrā}) — the \emph{-ā} on the end is this one.

Every sentence you own can now be asked. \kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಇದೆ} becomes \kn{ಚಹಾ} \kn{ಇದೆಯಾ} (\textquotedblleft{}is there tea?\textquotedblright{}); \kn{ನಿಮಗೆ} \kn{ಗೊತ್ತು} becomes \kn{ನಿಮಗೆ} \kn{ಗೊತ್ತಾ}. And the answer is the echo you learned first: \kn{ಹೌದು}, or \kn{ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Every statement in this book, asked.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gottu}, then \emph{gottā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nimage gottā?} — and answer it \emph{haudu} or \emph{gottilla}
  \item \emph{Say it:} take a sentence you already know and put \emph{-ā} on the end of it
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nānū}, then say \emph{nanagū}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{\kn{ಅ}} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{alla} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{bisilu}, \emph{ākāśa}, \emph{ajja}, \emph{bare}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What turns a Kannada statement into a yes-or-no question? (The ending \textbf{-\kn{ಆ}}.) Ask somebody whether they know.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[alvā]{\kn{ಅಲ್ವಾ} (alvā) — isn't it?}

\label{lesson:KA-C69-isnt-it}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: which ending makes a question, and what does \emph{gottā} ask?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಅಲ್ವಾ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಅಲ್ವಾ}} (\emph{alvā}) — \textquotedblleft{}isn't it?\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}right?\textquotedblright{}

Two things you already have, pushed together. \kn{ಅಲ್ಲ} (\textquotedblleft{}is not\textquotedblright{}) takes the question ending \textbf{-\kn{ಆ}} and becomes \kn{ಅಲ್ಲವಾ} (\emph{allavā}) — \textquotedblleft{}is it not?\textquotedblright{}. In ordinary speech that flattens to \textbf{\kn{ಅಲ್ವಾ}}, and it is the flattened one you will hear.

\textbf{\kn{ಇದು} \kn{ಒಳ್ಳೆಯ} \kn{ಪುಸ್ತಕ}, \kn{ಅಲ್ವಾ}?} (\emph{idu oḷḷeya pustaka, alvā?}) — \textquotedblleft{}this is a good book, isn't it?\textquotedblright{}

Register, plainly: \kn{ಅಲ್ವಾ} is spoken Kannada. Written Kannada says \kn{ಅಲ್ಲವೇ}. This book teaches the everyday spoken variety throughout, so \kn{ಅಲ್ವಾ} is what you get here.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: asking for agreement, not information}]
Somebody who says \kn{ಅಲ್ವಾ} usually knows the answer already; they are inviting you to agree, and they expect \kn{ಹೌದು}.

That makes it the cheapest politeness move in the language. A flat statement can land as a correction; the same statement with \kn{ಅಲ್ವಾ} on the end hands the other person a share of it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A question you can ask about anything, and a tag that softens it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{alla}, then \emph{allavā}, then \emph{alvā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{idu oḷḷeya pustaka, alvā?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} say something true about this room and add \emph{alvā}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gottā}, then answer it
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{hālū illa, nīrū illa} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{candra}, \emph{kēḷu}, \emph{nōḍu}, \emph{koḍu}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಅಲ್ವಾ} ask for? (Agreement.) Which two pieces is it made of? (\emph{alla} and the question ending \textbf{-\kn{ಆ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yāke]{\kn{ಯಾಕೆ} (yāke) — why?}

\label{lesson:KA-C69-why}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what does \emph{alvā} invite the other person to do?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಯಾಕೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಯಾಕೆ}} (\emph{yāke}) — \textquotedblleft{}why?\textquotedblright{}

The question words came in a set: \kn{ಯಾರು} (\emph{yāru}, \textquotedblleft{}who\textquotedblright{}), \kn{ಎಲ್ಲಿ} (\emph{elli}, \textquotedblleft{}where\textquotedblright{}), \kn{ಏನು} (\emph{ēnu}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}). \kn{ಯಾಕೆ} is the one the set was missing, and it is the one a short conversation runs out of first.

\textbf{\kn{ಯಾಕೆ}?} on its own is a whole turn. Somebody says they are not coming; you say \kn{ಯಾಕೆ}, and you have asked the only question that matters.

You will also meet \textbf{\kn{ಏಕೆ}} (\emph{ēke}) for the same word. It is the careful, written form; \kn{ಯಾಕೆ} is what gets said. Keep the two side by side — the word for \textquotedblleft{}because\textquotedblright{} is built on the written one, and it is not far off.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four question words now, and the one that opens a reason. Asking why is half of a conversation; the other half is the answer, and that is next.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yāke}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yāru}, \emph{elli}, \emph{yāke} — three questions in a row
  \item \emph{Say it:} somebody tells you \emph{illa} — ask them why
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{alvā}, then use it on the end of a sentence
  \item \emph{Recall:} the whole chapter — \emph{\kn{ೂ}}, \emph{gottā}, \emph{alvā}, and this one
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{gottilla} once more
  \item \emph{Recall:} from much earlier — say \emph{cukki}, \emph{nillu}, \emph{kuḷitukō}, \emph{bā}, and say what each one means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಯಾಕೆ} ask? (\textquotedblleft{}Why?\textquotedblright{}) What is its careful written twin? (\emph{ēke}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la]{\kn{ಲ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S137-letter-la}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{◌ೂ} — what does it do to the consonant it sits on?

One character this time — and it is the one standing in the middle of both of Kannada's negatives.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಲ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಲ}} — \emph{la}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{l}, it is \textbf{la}. Kannada has a second l as well — the thicker \kn{ಳ} you already trace — and the two are different letters for different sounds, not a matter of handwriting.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ಲ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅಲ್ಲ}} \emph{alla} — is not (that)
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}} \emph{illa} — there is not
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹಲ್ಲು}} \emph{hallu} — a tooth
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಕಾಲು}} \emph{kālu} — a leg
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಲ}}
Put your pen on \kn{ಲ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{ಲ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಅಲ್ಲ}  ·  \kn{ಇಲ್ಲ}  ·  \kn{ಹಲ್ಲು}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಲ} three times, saying \emph{la} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{ಲ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಲ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{la}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
